extracted.intended_audience: political science researchers / prospective APSR authors (scholarly authors submitting manuscripts to the American Political Science Review)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines describing the five distinct publication tracks at the American Political Science Review, including what kinds of contributions each track is intended to publish and important formatting, timing, and evaluation criteria for submissions. Useful for authors deciding which track fits their manuscript and for reviewers/editors assessing submissions under each track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular Articles: original work to advance understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular Articles: original work to advance understanding of important issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Notes: shorter, focused contributions; reclassification allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Research Notes track is designed for articles that are shorter and more focused than a Research Article. Submissions may be submitted initially as Research Notes or, during the review process – and by agreement of the handling editor and the corresponding author – reclassified as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research Notes should aim to be 7,000 words or less (not including references or online appendices) on final publication. The journal cannot reconsider submissions previously submitted and rejected. The track is intended to encourage authors to submit more focused contributions and to encourage reviewers to update their standards when assessing these papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered Reports: pre-analysis review and in-principle acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Registered Report, the theory, methods, and proposed analyses are reviewed before the research is completed. If the design is considered promising enough, the journal agrees to publish the paper so long as the ultimate implementation closely follows the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered Reports must be submitted prior to any data analysis. This format emphasizes excellent research design, reduces incentives that favor particular results, and allows authors to receive reviewer feedback at the design stage. Acceptance is conditional on faithful implementation of the reviewed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntheses: comprehensive synthetic pieces that push a field forward
rubrics_metrics.description: The Synthesis track is designed for articles that provide a synthetic view of a topic. These are not simply reviews of who said what; they are comprehensive attempts to grapple with an important research question and to push it forward. A Synthesis should summarize the state of the field, identify strengths and weaknesses, track progress, and point the way toward productive avenues of future research. Authors should touch upon theory, methodology, and findings (though they may choose to focus on one of these aspects). Typically, there is some original data analysis. Meta-analyses and “meta-models” are welcomed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For initial submission, the journal encourages (but does not require) a prospectus format to allow an initial decision while saving author time. Manuscripts may be submitted at any time, but initial submissions for this track are reviewed only once a year (in September); to be eligible for consideration submissions should be complete by October 1. At publication, a Synthesis should be less than 11,000 words (not including references or online appendices) — described as a soft target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replications and Reappraisals: re-evaluation that substantively enhances understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Replications and Reappraisals reevaluate works published in the APSR or influential works published in other journals. Submissions can show mistakes in published work, reanalyze existing data with improved methods, or bring new data to bear on the same question. They can interrogate quantitative or qualitative work, formal theory, or political theory, and may critique or support the conclusions of the original article. The primary criterion in assessing whether a replication/reappraisal should be published is whether it substantively enhances our understanding of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no strict word limit for this track, but authors are encouraged to be concise and to the point; most such articles require less than 6,000 words. The Journal will also solicit proposals for replication for a random set of articles published by the current editorial team; selected proposals, once completed, will be reviewed along similar lines as a registered report (i.e., proposal review and conditional acceptance process). This track accepts work that corrects mistakes, improves methods, or brings new data to bear.
